comment: THis section presents a fairly accurate architectural description of what a mature DHIS2 national HMIS deployment already does. But, HMIS/RHIS is reduced to a ‘shared application component’ and explicitly declared non-foundational, even within business service layer. This underestimates the infrastructural role of a national DHIS2 platform: it provides shared organisational hierarchies, metadata, aggregate and event/person data, indicators, analytics/GIS, data quality and approval workflows, offline collection, notifications, APIs, extensions and a user/support ecosystem across programmes. While these could come from other sources, in current landscape, HMIS are the source of truth for facility registries and indicator construction. Public-health informatics treats RHIS as the people–process–information–technology system through which routine decisions are made—not merely an application consuming LHR data.

reviewer.name: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO)
reviewer.organisation: HISP Centre at University of Oslo

public.suggestedRevision: Redefine HMIS/RHIS as a governed socio-technical public-health information infrastructure. Distinguish its software platform from the wider RHIS, but recognise that the platform may supply shared foundational capabilities.
